connections.how: Brand Visibility sends aggregate AI-agent activity (from CDN logs, by URL and host) into CJA through an Experience Platform source. AI-referred visits and conversions come from CJA's own web data, and Brand Visibility reads those results for its business impact view.

gain.title: AI-agent activity and observed referral outcomes
gain.text: Four separate measures. AI-agent activity (from CDN logs) and monitored visibility (tracked prompts) are what Brand Visibility adds; AI-referred visits and conversions come from your client's CJA web data, which ordinary referrer reporting can show without it; lift comes only from a test. The data is aggregate: nothing ties a person to an AI mention.

RT01.name: Data model, schema and identity design
RT01.scope: Run use-case workshops, map your client's entities into profile, event and lookup schemas, and choose the identity namespaces and primary identities the profile will merge on.
RT01.evidence: it is important to follow best practices for data modeling when designing your schemas

RT02.name: Data sources and ingestion setup
RT02.scope: Connect the agreed sources such as CRM, loyalty, commerce and web or app events, map fields to XDM, enable datasets for Profile and check that the first loads build the expected profiles.
RT02.evidence: You can ingest data from a variety of sources such as Adobe applications, cloud-based storages, databases, and many others.

references.title: Adobe Experience Platform End-to-End Example Workflow

RT03.name: Profile and merge policy configuration
RT03.scope: Set the merge method and dataset priority in the default merge policy, review how the identity graph links records, and check sample profiles against source data.
RT03.evidence: merge policies are the rules that Experience Platform uses to determine how data will be prioritized

RT04.name: Audience build and destination activation
RT04.scope: Build the starting audiences, connect the agreed destinations, choose the identities and attributes to send, then schedule and test the first activations.
RT04.evidence: After you configure your destination, you can activate audiences in multiple ways

references.title: Adobe Experience Platform End-to-End Example Workflow

RT05.name: Governance, access and sandbox setup
RT05.scope: Set up roles, permissions and development and production sandboxes, apply schema-field usage labels, enable the agreed data usage policies, and confirm activations respect those policies.
RT05.evidence: assist your team with the right permissions, access controls, and sandbox configurations

RT06.name: Monthly audience and dataflow operations
RT06.src: Adobe Experience Platform end-to-end example workflow
RT06.scope: Each month, review source and destination dataflows and alerts, fix failed runs, retire or refresh audiences, and add destinations as new use cases come in.
RT06.evidence: Experience Platform allows you to track how data is being processed through the use of dataflows

JO01.name: Access, sandbox and channel setup
JO01.scope: Set up roles and sandboxes, delegate the sending subdomains, and create the email and other channel configurations, IP pools and suppression and allowed lists.
JO01.evidence: Define all the technical parameters required for email, mobile messages, push notifications, web push, direct mail, and other channels

JO02.name: Journey events, data sources and actions
JO02.scope: Configure the identity namespaces, profile-enabled schemas and datasets the journeys need, then the journey events, data sources, custom actions and test profiles.
JO02.evidence: to be able to send messages in journeys, you must configure Data Sources, Events and Actions

JO04.name: Content templates and personalization
JO04.scope: Build reusable email and message templates and fragments, set up personalization and dynamic content, and preview rendering with test profiles.
JO04.evidence: Create reusable content templates and fragments to maintain brand consistency.

JO05.name: First journeys and campaigns
JO05.scope: Design, build, test and publish the starting journeys and campaigns, such as a welcome series, an abandoned cart journey and a scheduled campaign, with entry, wait and exit rules.

CE01.name: Store structure and Admin setup
CE01.src: Experience League: Store and site structure
CE01.scope: Plan your client's hierarchy of websites, stores and store views, create them in the Admin and set each store's root category and base URL. Set configuration values at the global, website or store view scope, choose the base, display and allowed currencies and update their rates, and create Admin user roles and accounts limited to the websites and stores each team needs.
CE01.evidence: You can create additional websites, stores, and store views, as needed.

CE02.name: Catalog import
CE02.src: Experience League: Options for importing a catalog
CE02.scope: Choose the import method for your client's catalog by its size and how often it changes: manual entry, the Admin CSV import, the bulk or asynchronous REST APIs, or the CSV REST API. Prepare and load the agreed product data. For an Admin CSV import, run Check Data, correct the problems listed, and review the import history and error file.
CE02.evidence: There are a few native methods for importing a catalog into Adobe Commerce.

CE03.name: Checkout, payment, tax and delivery settings
CE03.scope: Set the tax, checkout, shipping and payment settings in the Commerce Admin to your client's approved rules: tax classes, rules and rates, guest checkout and terms and conditions, the shipping origin, carriers and delivery methods, and the payment methods with their order status, currency and country settings. Run test transactions in sandbox mode before the store goes live.
CE03.evidence: The sales configuration settings determine checkout and tax settings, payment and shipping options, sales email and PDF print-outs, and Google API settings.

CE04.name: Inventory sources and stocks setup
CE04.src: Experience League: Introduction to Inventory Management
CE04.scope: Create a source for each of your client's fulfillment locations, add stocks that map their websites to those sources, assign sources and quantities to products and check the salable quantity for each stock. Order the sources in each stock and configure the distance priority algorithm so shipment recommendations follow your client's fulfillment rules.
CE04.evidence: It provides tools in the Admin and command-line interface to configure inventory, track on-hand and aggregate salable quantities, protect inventory during checkout, and support order fulfillment.

CE05.name: Live Search setup
CE05.src: Experience League: Set up for success with Live Search
CE05.scope: Install the Live Search extension with Composer, connect it with your client's Commerce API keys, sync the catalog data and check the export. Set searchable and filterable attributes, facets, synonyms and search merchandising rules, then test search, category browse and filters on the storefront.
CE05.evidence: At this point, Admin users can set up, customize, and manage search facets, synonyms, and merchandising rules.
CE05.tier: Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 or later on cloud infrastructure or on-premises

CE06.name: B2B buyer and purchasing setup
CE06.scope: Enable company accounts, shared catalogs, B2B quotes and purchase orders in the Admin for your client, set the default B2B payment and shipping methods and payment on account, create the first company accounts with credit limits and shared catalogs with custom pricing, then test company roles, negotiable quotes and purchase order approval rules on the storefront.
CE06.evidence: When you enable company support, the shared catalog, B2B quote, B2B payment methods, and B2B shipping methods are enabled automatically.

CE07.name: Monthly maintenance and upgrades
CE07.scope: Each month, apply the patches your client needs with the Quality Patches Tool after testing them in a staging or development environment, plan and test the next Adobe Commerce upgrade with the Upgrade Compatibility Tool, review indexer configuration and site performance, and fix the issues found.
CE07.evidence: Apply, revert, and view general information about all Adobe Commerce patches.

CE08.name: Assessment and plan for the move to Commerce as a Cloud Service
CE08.src: Experience League: Migrate to Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service
CE08.scope: Run Adobe's Migration Assessment on your client's Commerce on Cloud or on-premises project, review its complexity rating with your client, list the custom code, extensions, data in custom tables and integrations to move, and agree the phases, the order of work and who does what between Adobe, your client and you.
CE08.evidence: Every Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service migration begins with an assessment.

CE09.name: Custom code rebuilt as App Builder apps for Cloud Service
CE09.src: Experience League: Migrate to Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service
CE09.scope: Rebuild each of your client's Commerce customizations and extensions that has no Cloud Service equivalent as an App Builder app using Commerce APIs, events and webhooks, start from the Commerce Developer Agent where it helps, review all generated code before production, and test each app against the agreed behavior.
CE09.evidence: Modernizing a store's customizations for this architecture is typically the most significant engineering effort in an Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service migration.

CE10.name: Data migration to Commerce as a Cloud Service
CE10.src: Experience League: Bulk data migration tool
CE10.scope: Set up your client's store settings and system configuration on the new instance first, move products, customers and orders with Adobe's bulk data migration tool, which Adobe provides through its Commerce Deployed Engineering engagement, build an App Builder job for data held in custom tables by third-party extensions, and reconcile record counts.
CE10.evidence: Configuration settings (store settings, system configuration) are not migrated automatically and must be set up on the target instance independently prior to migration.

CE11.name: Integrations and storefront rebuilt for Cloud Service
CE11.src: Experience League: Migrate to Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service
CE11.scope: Re-establish each of your client's back-office integrations on the new instance through APIs, events and App Builder, point the storefront at it and test every data flow end to end. The storefront build itself on Edge Delivery Services is the service Build the Commerce storefront on Edge.
CE11.evidence: Customizations are modernized into App Builder applications, storefronts are rebuilt on Edge Delivery Services (EDS), data is migrated into the new Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service tenant, and integrations are re-established using SaaS patterns.

CE12.name: Cutover to Commerce as a Cloud Service
CE12.src: Experience League: Migrate to Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service
CE12.scope: Plan and rehearse the cutover with your client, run the final data sync, switch traffic to Commerce as a Cloud Service, check orders, payments and search on the live store, retire the old platform and hand over to ongoing operation.
CE12.evidence: Cut over and operate - Switch traffic to Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service, decommission legacy systems, and transition into ongoing operation.

CE13.name: Multi-store, multi-brand and multi-region setup
CE13.src: Experience League: Store and site structure
CE13.scope: For each brand, store or region beyond the first, add its website, store and store views on the same Admin, a store view for each language, its allowed currencies and rates, its tax rules, the inventory sources and stock that serve it, and its local payment and shipping options, then test an order in each.
CE13.evidence: Within each website, you can have multiple stores, and within each store, separate store views.

CE14.name: Search and merchandising configuration on Cloud Service
CE14.src: Experience League: Merchandising Services powered by catalog views and policies
CE14.scope: On Commerce as a Cloud Service, where Adobe installs and connects the search and catalog services, set your client's catalog views and policies, search facets, synonyms and merchandising rules, then test search, category browse and filters on the storefront.
CE14.evidence: Configure catalog views and policies to define storefront product assortments. Apply merchandising rules across all catalog views or tailor them to a specific view. Configure product recommendations, search facets, and synonyms.

CE15.name: B2B setup on Cloud Service
CE15.src: Experience League: Adobe Commerce feature comparison
CE15.scope: On Commerce as a Cloud Service, where the core B2B features come installed, turn on company accounts, shared catalogs, quotes and purchase orders for your client, create the first company accounts with credit limits and custom pricing, and test company roles, quotes and approvals.
CE15.evidence: Full B2B capabilities available after installation Pre-installed with core B2B features

CE16.name: Monthly on-premises hosting operations
CE16.src: Experience League: Adobe Commerce on-premises installation overview
CE16.scope: Each month, run your client's on-premises Commerce servers: capacity planning and scaling, backups and disaster recovery tests, monitoring and alerts, and security patches for the operating system, PHP, database and middleware.
CE16.evidence: Capacity planning, auto scaling, clustering, backups, disaster recovery

ACO01.name: Commerce Optimizer instance and user setup
ACO01.src: Experience League: Get started with Adobe Commerce Optimizer
ACO01.scope: Set up your client's sandbox and production Commerce Optimizer instances, match each to the commerce and storefront environments of the same kind, add users in the Adobe Admin Console with the roles each team needs, and record the instance IDs and endpoints.
ACO01.evidence: Connect sandbox Optimizer instances to non-production commerce and storefront environments. Connect production Optimizer instances to production commerce and storefront environments.

ACO02.name: Catalog views, policies and price books in Commerce Optimizer
ACO02.src: Experience League: Adobe Commerce Optimizer overview
ACO02.scope: Design your client's catalog views for each brand, market, language or sales channel, the policies that filter what each view shows, and the price books each view uses, then check each view returns the agreed products and prices.
ACO02.evidence: Within Adobe Commerce Optimizer, you can manage your catalog by creating catalog views and policies that best define your business goals.

ACO03.name: Search, recommendations and merchandising in Commerce Optimizer
ACO03.src: Experience League: Adobe Commerce Optimizer overview
ACO03.scope: Set your client's search facets, synonyms and merchandising rules, add the product recommendations agreed for each page type, check storefront events arrive, and train the merchandisers to run them.
ACO03.evidence: In addition, the merchandiser can provide personalized experiences to drive traffic and engagement using product discovery, recommendations​, and intelligent merchandising.

MBI02.name: Data warehouse tables and calculated columns in Commerce Intelligence
MBI02.scope: Choose the tables and columns your client's reports need, set them to sync in the Data Warehouse Manager, and build the calculated columns for the agreed measures, such as customer lifetime value and repeat orders.
MBI02.evidence: Using the Data Warehouse Manager, you can manage table and column sync settings, drill down into a table's schema, and create calculated columns to use in reports.

MBI03.name: Commerce Intelligence dashboards and reports
MBI03.scope: Build the dashboards and reports your client's teams agreed, such as sales, customers, products and acquisition sources, check each number against Commerce, and walk the teams through reading and filtering them.
MBI03.evidence: Adobe Commerce Intelligence Dashboards give you a quick view of your store's performance and sales activity at a glance.

MBI04.name: Scheduled report emails and exports from Commerce Intelligence
MBI04.src: Experience League: Share data from a chart
MBI04.scope: Set up the scheduled emails your client's teams want from Commerce Intelligence dashboards, and show them how to export chart data to a CSV or Excel file.
MBI04.evidence: learn how to export and share data from a chart to a .csv or Excel file.

MBI05.name: Other data into Commerce Intelligence by file or API
MBI05.scope: Bring in the other data your client's reports need: upload agreed CSV files on a schedule, or write scripts that send data through the Adobe API, then join it to the Commerce tables in the data warehouse.
MBI05.evidence: There are four ways to get your data into Commerce Intelligence: connect a database, connect a SaaS integration, upload a .csv file, or use the Adobe API.

MK01.evidence: Set up Domain Keys Identified Mail (DKIM) and 2 separate CNAMEs for deliverability and email tracking links.

MK02.name: CRM sync and field mapping
MK02.src: Experience League: Sync fields for the native CRM connectors
MK02.scope: Agree the field mapping with the CRM admin before the first sync, connect Marketo Engage to Salesforce or Dynamics, choose which fields sync or stay hidden, and check that the sync is running correctly.
MK02.evidence: This tutorial walks you through how the sync works, setting up the sync to get the right data flowing

MK03.name: Program templates, emails and landing pages
MK03.src: Experience League: Plan for a new Marketo Engage implementation
MK03.scope: Design the program templates the team will clone (webinar, nurture, newsletter, event), with My Tokens, and build the branded email templates, landing pages and forms in Design Studio.
MK03.evidence: Developing email templates and landing pages.

MK04.name: Lead scoring, lifecycle and data hygiene
MK04.src: Experience League: Plan for a new Marketo Engage implementation
MK04.scope: Run a data audit, build the program that standardizes incoming data, and model lead scoring and the lead lifecycle with marketing and sales, through to the MQL handoff.

MK05.name: User training and setup documentation
MK05.src: Experience League: Plan for a new Marketo Engage implementation
MK05.scope: Train the marketing users on programs, smart campaigns and templates, and document the new instance setup so the team can run it after launch.
MK05.evidence: Conducting training sessions and/or materials for Users

MK06.name: Monthly Marketo instance review
MK06.src: Experience League: Auditing an inherited Marketo Engage instance
MK06.scope: Each month, review Admin, Marketing Activities, Design Studio and Database for clean-up, deliverability and scoring changes, and agree the fixes with your client's Marketo owner.
MK06.evidence: the most important sections within Marketo Engage, including Admin, Marketing Activities, Design Studio, and Database

MK08.name: Marketo Engage lead scoring and data hygiene
MK08.src: Experience League: Plan a new Marketo Engage implementation
MK08.scope: Audit lead data, standardize agreed fields, set up lead scoring and test the handoff to sales with representative leads.

MK07.name: Email program and preference migration from another platform
MK07.src: Experience League: View Blocked People in a Smart Campaign
MK07.scope: Inventory your client's active email programs, subscription types and suppression records, and agree which choice wins when sources or the CRM conflict. Import the people and their choices into Marketo Engage, set Unsubscribed, Marketing Suspended or Blocklisted with Change Data Value flow steps, so an unsubscribe covers every record with the same email address, and mark addresses that hard bounced on the old platform as Email Invalid. Set up the subscription center, rebuild the active programs with no marketing email set as operational, and check the first migrated send's blocked people and that no suppressed address is among its recipients.
MK07.evidence: Blocked people in the Marketo Engage database are marked blocklisted, unsubscribed, marketing suspended, or have an invalid or empty email.
MK07.ext: exports of people, subscription choices and suppression records from the current email platform

XT07.name: Marketo Engage connected to Claude
XT07.src: Experience League: Marketo Engage MCP Server
XT07.scope: Create a dedicated API-only user in your client's Marketo Engage with only the permissions the team needs and its credentials in LaunchPoint, confirm with the Marketo administrator that the instance is enabled for this access, set up Claude Desktop (with Adobe's helper file and Node.js on each computer) or Claude Code for the pilot users, test first in a sandbox with a request that changes nothing, agree which changes may be asked for in Claude, and write the starter requests and a one-page guide.
XT07.evidence: Use a dedicated API user in Marketo with only the permissions required for your work.

MK09.name: Marketo Engage sandbox validation
MK09.scope: Configure an entitled sandbox for the agreed implementation tests. Scope test data and CRM connections, validate the programs and document the promotion steps.
MK09.evidence: A Marketo Engage sandbox is an additional instance used for testing purposes before implementation in the production environment.
