CO05.name: Overlap and measurement reporting enablement
CO05.scope: Train your client's team to read audience overlap insights, pick audiences to activate, add campaign IDs and create campaign summary and attribution reports in the Measure workspace.
CO05.evidence: Get insight into overlap percentages and the number of overlapping identities between your audiences and those of your collaborators.

CO06.name: Monthly collaboration operations
CO06.src: Experience League: Real-Time CDP Collaboration quick start guide
CO06.scope: Each month, add or retire audiences, tune refresh schedules to manage credit use, set up projects for new campaigns and run overlap and measurement reports with collaborators.
CO06.evidence: You can add or remove audiences and update the refresh schedule directly in Collaboration.

CO03.name: Audience sourcing from cloud data sources
CO03.src: Experience League: Real-Time CDP Collaboration quick start guide
CO03.scope: For audiences kept outside Experience Platform, prepare files to Adobe's audience specification with SHA256-hashed identifiers and the required metadata, then set up the data connection to Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Snowflake, Azure storage or a Databricks Delta Share.
CO03.evidence: Cloud-based audience files must follow the required schema outlined in the Audience Specification PDF.
CO03.ext: a cloud data source such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage or Snowflake

MM01.name: Access, roles and sandbox setup
MM01.src: Experience League: Marketing Campaign Analytics administration
MM01.scope: Create the Permissions role with the Marketing Campaign Analytics resource and its harmonized data, model and plan permissions, add the sandboxes and dataset and schema permissions, and assign users.
MM01.evidence: For Marketing Campaign Analytics to function properly, you must set the correct permissions.

MM02.name: Marketing data ingestion and schemas
MM02.src: Experience League: Ingest data overview (Marketing Campaign Analytics)
MM02.scope: Model schemas on the XDM ExperienceEvent or Summary Metrics classes, then ingest channel spend and effort, conversions and internal and external factors with consistent dates, granularity and channel fields, and validate the loads.
MM02.evidence: Date and granularity are mandatory fields in the underlying schema for all aggregate data ingested as datasets

MM03.name: Harmonized data, touchpoints and conversions
MM03.src: Experience League: Harmonize datasets overview (Marketing Campaign Analytics)
MM03.scope: Define harmonized fields, write dataset rules for each aggregate, event and factor dataset, define marketing touchpoints and conversions, then sync and check the harmonized data.
MM03.evidence: Set up dataset rules to map fields from your aggregate (factor or summary) or experience event datasets to harmonized fields.

MM04.name: Model build, training and validation
MM04.src: Experience League: Models overview (Marketing Campaign Analytics)
MM04.scope: Configure models with the conversion, touchpoints, lookback and training windows, factors and priors, turn on multi-touch attribution where agreed, and retrain until the fit suits the business.
MM04.evidence: Retraining and rescoring are an iterative process as new findings and information emerge and adjustments are needed

MM05.name: Budget plans and team enablement
MM05.src: Experience League: Plans overview (Marketing Campaign Analytics)
MM05.scope: Build the first budget plans with flight dates and channel constraints, compare scenarios, and train marketing and finance users to read model and plan insights.
MM05.evidence: Plans in Marketing Campaign Analytics allow you to allocate budgets by business unit and channel.

MM06.name: Monthly data refresh, rescoring and plans
MM06.src: Experience League: Models overview (Marketing Campaign Analytics)
MM06.scope: Each month, load new spend, conversion and factor data, rescore or retrain models, rebuild plans on the rescored models and report ROI and budget shifts to stakeholders.
MM06.evidence: Also, when data is added to the model, a manual rescore of the model is required.

GS01.name: Provisioning, roles and Brands permissions
GS01.src: Experience League: Get started with GenStudio for Performance Marketing
GS01.scope: Assign GenStudio licenses in the Admin Console to system managers, editors and collaborators, and create the user group and Admin Console project that Brands permissions need.
GS01.evidence: System administrators must complete additional set-up tasks before collaborators can edit or create Brands.

GS02.name: Brand, product and persona guidelines
GS02.src: Experience League: Get started with GenStudio for Performance Marketing
GS02.scope: Gather and tidy your client's brand, product and persona documents, upload or enter them with channel guidelines, logos, colors and tone of voice, then test generated output and publish.
GS02.evidence: Content editors and collaborators cannot begin their work until the foundational elements of your organization's brand identity are established.

GS03.name: Channel templates and approved assets
GS03.src: Experience League: Work with templates (GenStudio for Performance Marketing)
GS03.scope: Design and code responsive HTML templates for email, Meta and display, add Handlebars content placeholders, upload and test them, and load the approved assets editors will use into Content.
GS03.evidence: Adapt your HTML template using the Handlebars templating language.

GS04.name: Paid media connections and activation setup
GS04.src: Experience League: GenStudio for Performance Marketing Activate
GS04.scope: Connect your client's Meta, LinkedIn and Campaign Manager 360 accounts with the right ad account permissions, confirm historical data reaches Insights, and test activation into existing campaigns and ad sets.
GS04.evidence: A GenStudio system manager or editor must connect the ad account for each paid ad channel before you can activate

GS05.name: Editor training and first campaign launch
GS05.src: Experience League: GenStudio for Performance Marketing user roles and permissions
GS05.scope: Train editors and approvers on prompting, creating experiences, review and approval and activation, while running the first campaign end to end with your client's team.
GS05.evidence: the quality and success of generated content partially depend on the quality of the brand guidelines your organization has uploaded

GS06.name: Monthly content refresh from Insights
GS06.src: Experience League: GenStudio for Performance Marketing Insights
GS06.scope: Each month, review Insights by campaign, media and attribute, generate and approve variants for weak ads, refresh hero content and update guidelines and templates as the brand changes.
GS06.evidence: Find content that is not performing well and use the integrated generative AI to create variations immediately

XT06.name: GenStudio for Performance Marketing in ChatGPT, Claude or Microsoft Copilot: connection and publishing rules
XT06.src: Experience League: GenStudio for Performance Marketing, AI Assistants
XT06.scope: Check your client's ChatGPT, Claude or Microsoft Copilot plan allows the connection, add Adobe's GenStudio address as a custom connector (in ChatGPT on the web with developer mode on; in Microsoft Copilot, following Microsoft's steps for a custom connection) and have each pilot user sign in with their Adobe ID and pick the Adobe organization, test questions about ad performance and a draft from a template, agree who may publish an approved ad from a conversation, and write the starter requests and a one-page guide. Where a Coworker service on the same quote already set the publishing rule, this service reuses it.
XT06.evidence: Once connected, you can query ad performance, assemble creative, and publish approved ads through natural-language conversations.

EP01.name: Roles, Manager Hub and home page setup
EP01.src: Adobe Help: Roles and permissions in Adobe Express for Enterprise
EP01.scope: Agree with your client who manages the app, templates and social publishing, assign the predefined or custom Express roles in the Admin Console, and set the home banner, featured templates and featured brands in Manager Hub.
EP01.evidence: System Admins should work with their business counterparts to define the level of control required for Adobe Express users.

EP02.name: Brands with logos, colors, fonts and voice
EP02.scope: Build your client's brands in Express with logos, colors, fonts, graphics, written guidelines and brand voice, set which elements come first, and share each brand with the right view or edit access.
EP02.evidence: Set up a brand in Adobe Express by naming it, choosing where to save it, and adding logos, colors, fonts, graphics, and guidelines.

EP03.name: Locked templates with brand controls
EP03.src: Adobe Help: Create custom templates with brand controls
EP03.scope: Convert your client's approved designs into shared templates with locked elements, allowed brands for colors and fonts, and set locations for replacement images, organized in projects.
EP03.evidence: Create reusable templates with brand restrictions and share them with team members for faster, more reliable template creation and remixing

EP04.name: Review and approval on templates
EP04.src: Adobe Help: Add review and approval workflows to templates
EP04.scope: Add the simple review inside Express to your client's templates, with up to three approvers each, and agree who approves which kind of content.
EP04.evidence: In the Add name or email section, enter up to three approvers who are part of your Teams or Enterprise account.

EP07.name: Training for template owners and members
EP07.src: Adobe Help: Organization custom templates, sharing, and visibility
EP07.scope: Train your client's template managers on brands, locks and sharing, and members on finding and remixing organization templates, including how sharing and search settings decide who sees a template.
EP07.evidence: Organization custom templates in Adobe Express let organizations share branded or reusable templates.

EP08.name: Monthly template refresh and usage review
EP08.src: Adobe Help: Check custom templates usage
EP08.scope: Review how often your client's custom templates are previewed and reused each month, retire the ones nobody uses, and add or update templates and brand elements.
EP08.evidence: View analytics for your custom templates and download as CSV to understand how often they are being discovered and reused by others.

EP05.name: Bulk creation from a spreadsheet
EP05.src: Adobe Help: Create designs in bulk
EP05.scope: Prepare designs and a CSV file so your client's team creates up to 249 variations in one pass, with each text and image element connected to a spreadsheet column.
EP05.evidence: Learn how to use the Bulk create feature in Adobe Express to quickly create up to 249 variations of a chosen design by easily swapping the text and assets.

EP06.name: Social publishing and scheduling setup
EP06.scope: Give the social publishing capability to the right people, connect your client's social accounts, and set up Content Scheduler to plan, preview, schedule and publish posts.
EP06.evidence: Save time with Content Scheduler in Adobe Express, which lets you plan, preview, schedule, and publish to all your social media channels with one click.

FR01.name: Admin Console users and account roles
FR01.src: Adobe Help: Manage Frame.io account roles
FR01.scope: Add your client's users to Frame.io through the Admin Console, decide who is a Content Admin and who is a Member, and document how people are added and removed.
FR01.evidence: Account roles apply across your entire Frame.io organization and determine whether users have administrative access to all public resources or need explicit invitations to access specific content.

FR02.name: Workspaces, projects and permission design
FR02.src: Adobe Help: Manage Frame.io account roles
FR02.scope: Design your client's workspaces, projects and restricted folders around teams and campaigns, and set the permissions each group inherits so people see only the work they should.
FR02.evidence: Understanding both account roles and the inheritance model helps you design an access control strategy that balances administrative efficiency with appropriate security boundaries.

FR03.name: Review shares, branding and security settings
FR03.scope: Set up how your client shares work for review: branded share pages and a default share template, required passphrases, default link expiry and download controls, and where the plan includes Secure Sharing, shares limited to named people and authorized domains.
FR03.evidence: Custom branded shares ... Passphrase-protected shares ... Share link expiration

FR07.name: Onboarding and training for editors and reviewers
FR07.src: Adobe Help: Frame.io and Creative Cloud for enterprise plans FAQ
FR07.scope: Train your client's editors, producers and reviewers on uploading, commenting, comparing versions and sharing, and invite the first teams into their projects.
FR07.evidence: Your administrator sets up the Frame.io account and invites team members to collaborate effectively.

FR08.name: Monthly Frame.io administration
FR08.src: Adobe Help: Manage Frame.io account roles
FR08.scope: Add and remove users, adjust account roles and project access, and watch storage use against the plan each month for your client.
FR08.evidence: System admins can modify account roles in the Admin Console or Frame.io's User Management page.

FR04.name: Watermark templates and rights protection
FR04.scope: Create watermark templates for your client's review shares, and where the plan includes them, switch on session-based or forensic watermarking and Digital Rights Management for sensitive work.
FR04.evidence: Digital Rights Management (DRM) ... Forensic Watermarking ... Session-based Watermarking

FR05.name: Custom metadata fields for assets
FR05.scope: Define the custom metadata fields your client's teams need on assets, such as campaign, status and usage rights, so work can be sorted, filtered and handed on with the same labels.
FR05.evidence: Anchored in an all-new, powerful metadata framework, teams can now use Frame.io to customize any creative workflow centered on media assets.

FR06.name: API automation with a service account
FR06.src: Adobe Help: Automate your setup using Frame.io server-to-server support
FR06.scope: Create a server-to-server project in the Adobe Developer Console for your client and build automations on the Frame.io API and webhooks, such as uploads, comments or status changes, without using a user license.
FR06.evidence: By creating a Service Account in the Adobe Developer Console, you establish secure API connections that don't consume user seats in your organization.

CC01.name: Admin Console product profiles and users
CC01.scope: Set up your client's product profiles by role, department or team, assign users and groups to them, and name the profile admins who manage assignments.
CC01.evidence: Product profiles link products to users. Assigning a user to a profile gives them access to the related Adobe apps and services.

CC02.name: Deployment packages with apps and plugins
CC02.scope: Build managed packages for your client's Windows and macOS devices with the chosen apps, versions, update settings and Marketplace plugins, and test them before IT deploys them.
CC02.evidence: Managed packages allow administrators to control which Adobe applications and versions are deployed, when updates are applied, and which configuration settings are included in the deployment.

CC03.name: Creative Cloud Libraries in business storage
CC03.src: Adobe Help: Creative Cloud Libraries in business storage
CC03.scope: Create projects in your client's business storage and build shared libraries of logos, colors, type styles and graphics in them, so the organization owns the libraries and designers pick up approved elements inside the apps.
CC03.evidence: Creative Cloud Libraries accelerate work by reducing clicks in the creative process, making it easy for designers to use the right assets and for organizations to control the use of assets.

CC04.name: Sharing policy and services by profile
CC04.scope: Agree with your client how company content may be shared outside the organization, set the asset sharing policy in the Admin Console, and switch optional services on or off for each product profile.
CC04.evidence: As a system administrator, you can restrict sharing features within Creative Cloud and Document Cloud to ensure that sensitive content reaches only appropriate external recipients.

CC06.name: Training on libraries and connected workflows
CC06.src: Adobe Help: Creative Cloud Libraries in business storage
CC06.scope: Train your client's creative teams on shared libraries, cloud documents and the panels that connect the apps to the rest of their Adobe products.
CC06.evidence: Libraries in projects allow you to easily and quickly share collections of elements with your organization or collaborators.

CC05.name: Custom fonts for the organization
CC05.src: Adobe Help: Upload and manage custom fonts
CC05.scope: Accept the Custom fonts offer in the Admin Console, upload the fonts your client is licensed to use, and set which users receive them.
CC05.evidence: Add a font once, and Creative Cloud syncs it to your users' devices for use in supported apps.

CC07.name: Monthly Creative Cloud administration
CC07.src: Adobe Help: Manage services in the Admin Console
CC07.scope: Update packages for new app versions, adjust product profiles and services, and add or remove users each month for your client.
CC07.evidence: You can enable and disable services at the product profile level, not for individual user accounts.

WP01.name: Licenses, access levels and layout templates
WP01.src: Experience League: Get started with Adobe Workfront Planning
WP01.scope: Assign Planning licenses and permissions to your client's users, add the license types to their access levels, and assign a layout template that shows Planning to Contributor and Light users.
WP01.evidence: Assign users Workfront and Planning licenses and Workfront Planning permissions that would allow them to either view or create objects in Workfront Planning.

WP02.name: Workspaces and record type model
WP02.scope: Model how your client plans work: design the workspaces, the record types (such as campaigns, products, regions and personas), their fields and how they connect, then build them from scratch or from a template.
WP02.evidence: A workspace is a collection of record types used by a team and represents the team's work lifecycle.

WP03.name: Records and fields imported from spreadsheets
WP03.src: Experience League: Create record types (Workfront Planning)
WP03.scope: Clean your client's planning spreadsheets and import them as record types, fields and records, then check the connections between the imported records.
WP03.evidence: When you import a record type from a CSV or Excel file, you can also import records and fields.

WP04.name: Table, timeline and calendar views
WP04.src: Experience League: Manage record views (Workfront Planning)
WP04.scope: Build the shared views your client's teams and leaders use, such as a marketing calendar and a campaign timeline, with the filters, groupings and fields each audience needs.
WP04.evidence: You can view records in views of several formats that give you the flexibility to explore and understand information in the way that works best for you.

WP07.name: Rollout plan and training
WP07.src: Experience League: Get started with Adobe Workfront Planning
WP07.scope: Plan your client's rollout team by team, teach the Planning terms and how to add, connect and view records, and hand over a short guide for workspace owners.
WP07.evidence: Although Workfront Planning is part of Workfront, it comes with proprietary concepts and terminology.

WP08.name: Monthly Planning administration
WP08.src: Adobe Help: Adobe Workfront product description
WP08.scope: Add record types, fields and views as your client's planning changes, tidy records and connections, and adjust sharing each month.
WP08.evidence: It lets organizations define strategy, manage campaigns, centrally manage marketing metadata, and build data visualizations that connect plans directly to execution.

WP05.name: Request forms with approvals
WP05.src: Experience League: Adobe Workfront Planning requests
WP05.scope: Create a request form for the record types your client takes requests for, add approval rules by field value, and share the forms with the people who submit them.
WP05.evidence: You can create a request form for each record type, share it with users and they can add new records by completing and submitting the form.

WP06.name: Planning reports and dashboards
WP06.src: Experience League: Adobe Workfront Planning reporting
WP06.scope: Build reports on your client's Planning records in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard, or prepare the Planning data in Workfront Data Connect for their own reporting tool.
WP06.evidence: You can create reports from Adobe Workfront Planning using the Workfront Canvas Dashboard or Workfront Data Connect which uses Snowflake technology.

FP01.name: Creative Production access, roles and API credentials
FP01.src: Adobe Firefly help: Bulk actions overview
FP01.scope: Assign Firefly Creative Production (or Firefly Services) to your client's users and groups in the Admin Console, agree who authors workflows and who only runs them, create the Developer Console project and credentials for API use, and agree how Operations are tracked against the contract.
FP01.evidence: Your organization must have a Firefly Services or a Firefly Creative Production entitlement to access Creative Production.

FP02.name: Bulk presets: remove background, crop and color grade
FP02.src: Adobe Firefly help: Bulk actions overview
FP02.scope: Set up the preset bulk actions for your client's production team: background removal and replacement, crop sizes and aspect ratios for each channel, and custom color presets, then run a pilot batch and write the house rules for file naming and review.
FP02.evidence: These out-of-the-box preset workflows grant you the power to scale asset production from one image or video to thousands with just a few clicks.

FP03.name: Production workflows from Adobe's templates
FP03.src: Adobe Firefly help: Workflow templates on the Creative Production home page
FP03.scope: Start from Adobe's workflow templates for banners and product assets, fit them to your client's formats, copy and offer variants and markets, test them on sample assets and confirm the outputs with the creative lead.
FP03.evidence: The Workflows tab on the Creative Production home page has various workflow templates for specific production use cases, organized by Banners at Scale and Product Assets

FP05.name: Published workflows run from your client's systems
FP05.src: Adobe Developer: Firefly Creative Production Workflow API
FP05.scope: Publish the validated workflows and connect your client's systems to the Creative Production Workflow API: credentials and tokens, batch runs with inputs passed as pre-signed URLs, status checks, per-asset results, retries for failures and where finished files are stored.
FP05.evidence: The Firefly Creative Production Workflow API lets you execute published workflows across multiple assets in one batch.

FP08.name: Governance, training and handover
FP08.src: Adobe Firefly help: Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise overview
FP08.scope: Write the operating rules (who authors, who publishes, who runs, how changes to a published workflow are approved), train your client's creative technologists and production team, and hand over a run book for each workflow.
FP08.evidence: Some organizations give workflow authoring and admin access to a smaller group of specialists while giving a broader group access to run published workflows, guided experiences, APIs, or bulk actions.

FP09.name: Monthly workflow operations and tuning
FP09.src: Adobe Firefly help: Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise overview
FP09.scope: Each month, review job status, logs and failed assets, rerun only what needs to change, tune workflow steps and templates as your client's formats and campaigns change, and report Operations used against the contract.
FP09.evidence: Review flagged items and rerun only what needs to change.

FP04.name: Custom production workflows in Workflow Builder
FP04.src: Adobe Firefly help: Add and connect nodes
FP04.scope: Turn one of your client's production playbooks into a workflow of its own: define the inputs, connect the generate, edit and transform nodes, add the outputs, then test and refine with sample assets until the results match the brief.
FP04.evidence: With workflows, you can combine input nodes (text, images, and videos), processing nodes (generate, edit, and transform), and output nodes (final deliverables) into automated sequences.

FP06.name: Firefly Services API automation
FP06.src: Adobe Firefly help: Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise overview
FP06.scope: Build direct calls to the Firefly Services APIs for jobs a workflow does not cover, such as image generation, Photoshop edits and renditions, InDesign data merge or Illustrator renditions, with credentials, error handling and Operations tracked for each job.
FP06.evidence: Access to Firefly Services APIs for headless and programmatic use cases.

FP07.name: Run-Workflow MCP for AI agents
FP07.src: Adobe Firefly help: Run-Workflow MCP overview
FP07.scope: Connect your client's approved AI tools (Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor) to the Run-Workflow MCP server with the token and API key from the organization's administrator, test the supported creative tasks, and write the rules for who may run them and where outputs are saved.
FP07.evidence: Run-Workflow MCP connects Model Context Protocol (MCP)-compatible AI agents and Adobe's creative workflow services.

FP10.name: 3D digital twin workflows: packshots, spin video and composite imagery
FP10.src: Adobe Firefly help: Use 3D digital twin workflows
FP10.scope: Set up Adobe's 3D digital twin starter templates for your client's products (standardized packshots, 360 degree spin video and composite imagery): load each product's USDZ model from local storage, Frame.io or AEM, set the camera angles, render settings and background prompts the templates offer, run a pilot on a first set of products and confirm the outputs with the creative lead.
FP10.evidence: All 3D Digital Twin workflows are available as starter templates in the Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise home page.
FP10.ext: a USDZ 3D model of each product

FM01.name: Custom Models access, trainers and projects
FM01.src: Adobe enterprise help: Assign users to Firefly custom models
FM01.scope: Assign a product administrator for Firefly Custom Models, create the trainer profile and user group in the Admin Console, give trainers a product that includes Firefly, and set up the projects that models will be stored and shared in.
FM01.evidence: Assign at least one product administrator for Firefly Custom Models to manage user entitlements and the models.

FM02.name: Training image sets and captions
FM02.src: Adobe Firefly help: Best practices for training custom models
FM02.scope: Choose with your client's brand team what each model should keep consistent (a subject or a style), select and clear 10 to 30 images for each model, upload them, and correct the captions, tags and model properties Firefly proposes until the dataset review is clean.
FM02.evidence: Selecting consistent, high-quality images and refining captions and tags helps improve the quality and consistency of generated results.

FM03.name: Model training, testing and publishing
FM03.src: Adobe Firefly help: Create and train custom models
FM03.scope: Train each model, test it with sample prompts against your client's brand guidelines, duplicate and train again where results fall short, then publish the models that pass so other users and apps can generate with them.
FM03.evidence: Training a custom model involves three key actions: upload, analyze, and train.

FM04.name: Prompt guide for each model
FM04.src: Adobe Firefly help: Prompt guidelines for custom models
FM04.scope: Write a short prompt guide for each model: the sample prompt, the Concept ID for subject models, the words that match the training captions, and examples of what the model does well and what it should not be asked for.
FM04.evidence: Your custom model already understands your aesthetic from training, so prompts should specify content details like subjects, poses, settings, and compositions.

FM05.name: Sharing, permissions and model governance
FM05.src: Adobe Firefly help: Share custom models
FM05.scope: Set who may edit, review or only generate with each model, organize models into projects so access is granted once, and write the rules for naming, versions, approval before publishing and deleting old models.
FM05.evidence: Invited collaborators receive different levels of access based on the permissions you assign.

FM06.name: Retraining on a newer Firefly image model
FM06.src: Adobe Firefly help: Retrain custom models
FM06.scope: Duplicate your client's existing models, review the training data and settings, train them on the latest Firefly image model, compare results with the originals and retire the old versions once the new ones are approved.
FM06.evidence: Enterprise users can retrain an existing model using the latest version of Firefly Image Models.

FM07.name: Monthly model upkeep
FM07.src: Adobe Firefly help: Retrain custom models
FM07.scope: Each month, review what teams generated with each model, refresh training sets and prompt guides as campaigns and products change, train new versions where needed and remove models nobody uses.
FM07.evidence: Adobe regularly releases new versions of Firefly Image Models to improve the quality and accuracy of generated images.

BN01.name: Brand sources gathered for Adobe's onboarding
BN01.src: Adobe Firefly help: Adobe Brand Intelligence overview
BN01.scope: Gather and tidy what Adobe's engineers need to load for each licensed brand: guidelines, design systems, approved assets, briefs and past review comments, with your client's brand team deciding which rules matter most and which campaigns, channels, products and audiences a check should offer.
BN01.evidence: It brings together brand guidelines, design systems, creative assets, human feedback, and approvals.

BN02.name: Validate checks built into your client's tools
BN02.src: Adobe Developer: Adobe Brand Intelligence APIs
BN02.scope: Connect the Validate API to the tool where your client's team finishes creative work: Developer Console credentials, uploading assets, submitting a batch, waiting for results, and showing each asset's findings to the people who fix them.
BN02.evidence: Validate assets in bulk - submit a batch of assets and receive structured pass/fail feedback per asset.

BN04.name: Validation pilot on live campaigns
BN04.src: Adobe Firefly help: Validate brand compliance
BN04.scope: Run a pilot on current campaign assets with your client's brand team: choose the campaign, channel, product and audience for each check, compare the findings with human review, and list for Adobe's engineers the rules that need tightening before rollout.
BN04.evidence: Use Validate to quickly check whether your content is compliant with your organization's brand identity and guidelines.

BN07.name: Reviewer training and rollout
BN07.src: Adobe Firefly help: Validate brand compliance
BN07.scope: Train your client's designers, reviewers and brand team to read findings, open the guideline behind each one, and approve, edit or reject suggestions, then roll the checks out team by team with a named owner for questions.
BN07.evidence: Your approval, edits, or rejection of each suggestion feeds back into the Adobe Brand Intelligence for continuous learning.

BN08.name: Monthly brand rule review
BN08.src: Adobe Firefly help: Adobe Brand Intelligence overview
BN08.scope: Each month, review the findings reviewers rejected or edited, collect new guidelines and campaign rules from your client's brand team, pass changes to Adobe's engineers, and report how many assets passed first time.
BN08.evidence: Instead of relying only on written guidelines, the system learns from your assets, past reviews, and team decisions, so your brand standards are applied consistently, every time.

BN03.name: Reviewer feedback loop
BN03.src: Adobe Developer: Brand Intelligence, Review Feedback
BN03.scope: Build the step where your client's reviewers accept, edit or reject each finding and add their own, send those decisions back through the API, and agree who reviews what so the checks improve with use.
BN03.evidence: After a validation invocation completes, reviewers can attach structured feedback to each item's validation findings.

BN05.name: Simulate in your client's chat assistant
BN05.src: Adobe Developer: Brand Intelligence Simulate, Using MCP
BN05.scope: Connect your client's chat assistant to the Simulate MCP server, test a first study on real creative with the templates and audience segments Adobe has set up, and write a short guide to choosing an objective, assets, template and audience.
BN05.evidence: This guide is for teams integrating Adobe Brand Intelligence Simulate into their own chat assistant via its MCP (Model Context Protocol) server.

BN06.name: Figma templates for assembled variants
BN06.src: Adobe Firefly help: Instruct to Assemble
BN06.scope: Prepare your client's Figma templates for the Adobe Brand Intelligence plugin, agree the contexts and assembly options with Adobe's engineers, run first batches of two or three variants, and check the results with the design lead before larger runs.
BN06.evidence: You can use Instruct to assemble in Figma via the Adobe Brand Intelligence plugin to quickly create multiple on-brand variants using predefined templates and brand guidelines.

AN01.name: Solution design and measurement plan
AN01.src: Experience League: Create a solution design document
AN01.scope: Run KPI and business-question workshops with your client's stakeholders, map each requirement to a dimension or metric and its Analytics variable, and write the solution design document your client's team keeps current.
AN01.evidence: A solution design document (also known as a solution design reference or business requirements document) is in essence the blueprint of your analytics implementation.

AN02.name: Report suites, variables and marketing channels
AN02.scope: Create the development and production report suites, enable and name the conversion variables, success events and props from the solution design, add processing rules and bot rules, and configure marketing channels and classification sets for campaign tracking codes.
AN02.evidence: Plan ahead by making a list of all your channels, so that all of your visitor hits are categorized to the right channel.

AN03.name: Data layer and Web SDK data collection
AN03.src: Experience League: Implement Adobe Analytics using the Web SDK tag extension
AN03.scope: Specify the data layer with your client's developers, set up the datastream, the tags property and the Web SDK extension, map data elements to Analytics variables, and validate in development before publishing to production.
AN03.evidence: This implementation path is the most straightforward and typically the recommended path for new Web SDK implementations.

AN04.name: Analysis Workspace projects and components
AN04.scope: Build the agreed Analysis Workspace projects for your client's priority questions, with the segments, calculated metrics and alerts behind them, and save company templates the team reuses.
AN04.evidence: Analysis Workspace allows you to build analyses quickly to gather insights and then share those insights with others.

AN05.name: Access, privacy labels and team training
AN05.src: Experience League: Product profiles for Adobe Analytics
AN05.scope: Set up product profiles in the Admin Console with the report suites, tools and components each team needs, assign identity and sensitivity labels to the report suite's variables, and train your client's analysts and business users on Analysis Workspace.
AN05.evidence: Product profiles are permission presets that product admins can assign to users within an organization.

AN08.name: Monthly analysis and implementation review
AN08.src: Experience League: Focused Review (after each website release)
AN08.scope: Each month, analyze your client's priority journeys and campaigns and report findings and next steps, and after each site release check that the metrics and dimensions behind the top KPIs still collect correctly.
AN08.evidence: If you consistently do this Focused Review after each website release, you'll find that your bi-annual Full Reviews are much easier.

AN06.name: Move an existing tags setup to Web SDK
AN06.src: Experience League: Web SDK upgrade assistant overview
AN06.scope: Move your client's Adobe Analytics tag extension setup to the Web SDK with Adobe's upgrade assistant: choose the rules and data elements, map the Analytics variables to XDM, review the Web SDK actions it adds, then test the new library and compare reports before publishing.
AN06.evidence: The Web SDK upgrade assistant helps you plan and execute the migration of your Adobe Analytics tags extension to the Adobe Experience Platform Web SDK.

AN07.name: Data feeds and Data Warehouse exports
AN07.scope: Set up the cloud account and location, create the hourly or daily data feed with the agreed columns, and schedule the Data Warehouse requests your client's data team needs.
AN07.evidence: Data feeds are a powerful way to get raw data out of Adobe Analytics.
AN07.ext: a cloud storage bucket on Amazon S3, Google Cloud Platform or Azure

MZ01.name: Admin Console users and tracking script rollout
MZ01.src: Experience League: Best practices for implementing Marketo Measure JavaScript
MZ01.scope: Add your client's admins and users in the Adobe Admin Console, claim each domain, and deploy the Marketo Measure JavaScript on every page and form of every tracked site, hardcoded or through a tag manager. Test that sessions and form fills are captured.
MZ01.evidence: Having the Marketo Measure JavaScript deployed correctly and comprehensively across your entire site(s) will ensure that the session data collected produces accurate touchpoint data.

MZ02.name: CRM package and connection
MZ02.src: Experience League: Marketo Measure CRM packageless integration
MZ02.scope: Install the Marketo Measure package in your client's Salesforce or Microsoft Dynamics sandbox and then in production, or set up the packageless route with a dedicated connected user. Connect the CRM, and set permission sets and page layouts.
MZ02.evidence: Through the standard Marketo Measure installation, you are required to install a Salesforce Package or a Microsoft Dynamics Managed Solution.

MZ03.name: Online and offline channel mapping
MZ03.src: Experience League: Online custom channel setup
MZ03.scope: Agree your client's UTM conventions, write the online channel rules and the offline channel mapping to CRM campaign types, set the campaign sync rules that turn campaign members into touchpoints, and check touchpoints land in the right channel and subchannel.
MZ03.evidence: To have accurate reporting, marketing channels must be set up to reflect your organization's UTM strategy.

MZ04.name: Ad platform connections and spend data
MZ04.scope: Connect your client's ad accounts with the right roles, set up tagging on ad URLs, switch on CRM campaign costs where used, and load spend for the channels that have no connection.
MZ04.evidence: Any Ad Account that you have connected to Marketo Measure through an API has its spend automatically pulled into Marketo Measure for ROI reporting.

MZ05.name: Stage mapping and attribution model setup
MZ05.src: Experience League: Best practices for stage mapping
MZ05.scope: Order your client's lead, contact and opportunity stages in Stage Mapping, choose the stages and weights for the custom attribution model where the subscription includes it, and review touchpoint and segment settings with marketing and sales operations.
MZ05.evidence: The validity of your Marketo Measure data relies on these stages being ordered correctly so that Marketo Measure can accurately understand your funnel and the progression of records throughout said funnel.

MZ06.name: Discover dashboards for marketing and sales
MZ06.scope: Walk your client's teams through the Discover dashboards, agree the filters and segments each group reads, and set the short list of revenue, pipeline and return views that leadership sees each month.
MZ06.evidence: Every dashboard has a range of filters, accompanied by the following controls for seamless navigation and customization.

MZ08.name: Monthly attribution upkeep
MZ08.scope: Each month, enable touchpoints for new CRM campaigns, load new spend, review channel mapping against new UTM values and domains, and report attributed pipeline and revenue by channel.
MZ08.evidence: Marketo Measure pulls almost everything that it needs from your CRM on a daily basis, but there are a few maintenance tasks you should schedule regularly to keep Marketo Measure humming along and outputting the most accurate information possible.

MZ07.name: Data warehouse access and BI report template
MZ07.src: Experience League: Data warehouse access, reader account
MZ07.scope: Give your client's analysts access to the data warehouse reader account, connect Adobe's Power BI or Tableau report template, and adapt it to your client's channels and date ranges.
MZ07.evidence: This is a read-only account that's available for your organization, not just an individual user.

AB01.name: Licenses, product profiles and sign-in
AB01.src: Adobe Help: Administer Acrobat Studio for enterprise
AB01.scope: Set up your client's Acrobat licensing in the Admin Console: the identity type and single sign-on, product profiles by team with the services each one gets, automatic assignment rules, and users added in bulk.
AB01.evidence: Admins can customize the Product Profiles for Acrobat Premium for enterprise, Acrobat Studio for enterprise, and Acrobat Reader Premium for enterprise.

AB02.name: Deployment packages and configured settings
AB02.src: Adobe Help: Create Acrobat-only deployment packages
AB02.scope: Build Acrobat packages in the Admin Console for each platform your client runs, set features and preferences with the Acrobat Customization Wizard before rollout, and agree with your client's IT team how updates are run.
AB02.evidence: After downloading the package, use the Acrobat Customization Wizard to configure Acrobat features and preferences before organization-wide deployment.

AB11.name: Training for users and administrators
AB11.src: Adobe Help: Administer Acrobat Studio for enterprise
AB11.scope: Train your client's teams on the Acrobat tasks that matter to them, such as editing, combining, protecting, redacting and requesting signatures, and administrators on licenses, packages and updates, with a handover guide.
AB11.evidence: Learn about Acrobat Studio for enterprise and how admins manage licensing, access, and security.

AB03.name: AI Assistant and PDF Spaces rollout
AB03.src: Adobe Help: Administer Acrobat Studio for enterprise
AB03.scope: Decide with your client which teams get the generative AI features, assign the licenses and product profile services, turn features off where your client's policy requires, and train teams on summaries, questions with citations and shared PDF Spaces.
AB03.evidence: AI Assistant requires a Named User license of Acrobat because the feature relies on cloud-based services linked to a user's identity.
AB03.tier: an Acrobat plan with AI Assistant

AB04.name: PDF Services API document automation
AB04.src: Adobe Developer: Acrobat Services APIs introduction
AB04.scope: Connect your client's application to the PDF Services API with server-side credentials and automate the document steps it needs, such as creating PDFs from Office files or HTML, text recognition, combining, compressing, protecting and exporting, with files read from and written to your client's own storage.
AB04.evidence: The PDF Services API offers a number of operations to programmatically manipulate documents and automate many different types of document workflows.

AB05.name: Document generation from Word templates
AB05.src: Adobe Developer: Document Generation API overview
AB05.scope: Build your client's contract, invoice or letter templates in Microsoft Word with template tags for text, tables, images and conditions, define the JSON data each one merges, and connect the Document Generation API so documents are produced from your client's system.
AB05.evidence: Document Generation API accepts a document template (with template tags) along with the input data to generate the final document.

AB06.name: PDF viewer embedded in your client's site
AB06.src: Adobe Developer: PDF Embed API overview
AB06.scope: Embed PDFs in your client's web pages or app with the PDF Embed API: a client ID for each domain, the embed mode, the tools visitors see, and viewer events passed to your client's analytics.
AB06.evidence: Adobe PDF Embed API allows you to embed a PDF viewer in your web applications with only a few lines of code.

AB07.name: Content extraction from PDFs
AB07.src: Adobe Developer: PDF Extract API overview
AB07.scope: Build the pipeline that sends your client's PDFs, native or scanned, to the PDF Extract API and loads the text, tables and figures it returns, as structured JSON or Markdown, into your client's search, data or AI systems.
AB07.evidence: The JSON output captures document structure information, such as the natural reading order of the various extracted elements and the layout of the elements on each given page.

AB08.name: PDF accessibility tagging at scale
AB08.src: Adobe Developer: PDF Accessibility Auto-Tag API overview
AB08.scope: Run your client's backlog of untagged PDFs through the Accessibility Auto-Tag API, read the tagging reports, and correct in Acrobat what tagging alone does not settle, such as alt text, complex tables, titles and reading order.
AB08.evidence: Automatic tagging is a good first step on a document's journey to full accessibility.

AB09.name: Electronic seals on issued documents
AB09.src: Adobe Developer: PDF Electronic Seal API overview
AB09.scope: Apply your client's organizational seal to invoices, statements and other official PDFs with the PDF Electronic Seal API, using a certificate hosted by a trust service provider that follows the Cloud Signature Consortium standard, with the seal's appearance set for each document type.
AB09.evidence: These digital certificates are issued by a CSC compliant Trust Service Provider (TSP).
AB09.ext: a trust service provider that hosts the certificate

AB10.name: PDF Services in Microsoft Power Automate flows
AB10.src: Experience League: Getting credentials for Microsoft Power Automate (Acrobat Services tutorial)
AB10.scope: Set up the Adobe PDF Services connector in your client's Microsoft Power Automate with its credentials, and build the flows that convert, combine, protect or generate documents on files in OneDrive, SharePoint or another storage connector.
AB10.evidence: Adobe PDF Services connector, as part of Adobe Acrobat Services, allows users to perform any of the actions available in Adobe PDF Services API within Microsoft Power Automate.
AB10.ext: Microsoft Power Automate with premium connectors

AB12.name: Monthly document automation upkeep
AB12.src: Adobe Developer: Licensing and usage limits (PDF Services API)
AB12.scope: Each month, review Document Transaction usage against your client's allowance, fix failed jobs, and update templates and flows as your client's documents change.
AB12.evidence: Adobe PDF Services API licensing is measured per Document Transaction which is based on the initial endpoint request (i.e., API call) and the digital output, with each operation in the table described below.

SG01.name: Account, users, groups and sign-in
SG01.src: Adobe Help: Manage Groups in Adobe Acrobat Sign
SG01.scope: Set up your client's account structure: groups for each business unit with their own settings, branding and templates, account and group administrators, users and their report access, and sign-in through the Adobe Admin Console with single sign-on.
SG01.evidence: Groups allow administrators to segment configuration within Adobe Acrobat Sign so different teams, processes, compliance requirements, or reporting structures can operate with their own settings, branding, and document access.

SG02.name: Account settings, branding and security
SG02.src: Adobe Help: Set up your Acrobat Sign company account
SG02.scope: Configure the account and group settings your client's policies call for: company name, logo and email branding, signature preferences, send settings, security settings and the external archive that receives a copy of every signed agreement.
SG02.evidence: This article provides an overview of the core features of branding, security settings, users, and templates to get you up and running.

SG03.name: Library templates and form fields
SG03.src: Adobe Help: Create a library template (Acrobat Sign)
SG03.scope: Turn your client's most used agreements into library templates with signature, date and data fields for each signer, built in the authoring environment or with text tags, and set who may use and edit each one.
SG03.evidence: Library templates let users create reusable, interactive documents.

SG04.name: Custom send workflows
SG04.src: Adobe Help: Custom Workflow Designer overview (Acrobat Sign)
SG04.scope: Build workflow templates in the Custom Workflow Designer for your client's regular agreement types: recipients and routing, the documents and fields included, email copies, expiration and passwords, with instructions for senders.
SG04.evidence: Use the Custom Workflow Designer to create custom Compose pages designed to support your documents, policies, and compliance requirements.

SG13.name: Training for senders, template authors and administrators
SG13.src: Experience League: Acrobat Sign tutorials, administrators overview
SG13.scope: Train your client's team by role: senders on sending, tracking and reminders, template authors on fields, templates and workflows, administrators on users, groups, settings and reports, with a handover guide.
SG13.evidence: These tutorials are designed for administrators who are past the installation phase, and are ready to start administering Acrobat Sign.

SG14.name: Monthly agreement reporting and template upkeep
SG14.scope: Each month, run agreement reports on completion rates and time to sign, review which templates and workflows stall, update templates and settings, and manage users and groups.
SG14.evidence: Run agreement reports to better understand the trends of your agreements in terms of what your agreement completion rate is, how long it takes, and which users or workflows seem to have greater success.

SG05.name: Web forms on your client's site
SG05.src: Adobe Help: Create a web form (Acrobat Sign)
SG05.scope: Create signable web forms for agreements people start themselves, with participants, counter-signers and signer authentication, and embed them on your client's website or share them as links.
SG05.evidence: A signable web form can be created to embed on your website (or sent as a web link), allowing multiple people to easily access your form or document and create an agreement.

SG06.name: Bulk sending from a recipient list
SG06.src: Adobe Help: Overview of Send in Bulk (Acrobat Sign)
SG06.scope: Set up Send in Bulk for agreements that go to many people at once: the parent template, the CSV file with recipients and merge fields, and how your client's team tracks the agreements it creates.
SG06.evidence: The Send in Bulk (SiB) feature allows users to create a one-use "parent" template of an agreement and supply a list of recipients.

SG07.name: Signer identity checks and digital signatures
SG07.src: Adobe Help: Acrobat Sign Digital Identity Gateway
SG07.scope: Choose the identity check for each kind of agreement your client sends, such as Acrobat Sign authentication, a phone or knowledge-based check or a provider on the Digital Identity Gateway, set the defaults by group, and enable digital signatures where the law or your client's policy asks for them.
SG07.evidence: The Adobe Acrobat Sign Digital Identity Gateway allows organizations to select from a wide variety of pre-configured third-party digital identity providers (IDP) and leverage the type of identity verification that best suits their functional, security, or compliance needs.
SG07.ext: a digital identity provider, where one is used

SG08.name: Retention rules and audit records
SG08.src: Adobe Help: Data governance overview (Acrobat Sign)
SG08.scope: Set data governance rules that delete agreements and their data after the retention period your client's records policy sets, and agree where signed copies and audit reports are kept before they are deleted.
SG08.evidence: Data governance in Adobe Acrobat Sign allows administrators to automatically delete agreements and associated data from the Acrobat Sign systems after a defined retention period.

SG09.name: API and webhook integration with your client's systems
SG09.src: Adobe Help: Acrobat Sign webhooks overview
SG09.scope: Connect your client's application to the Acrobat Sign REST API: the API application and OAuth, agreements sent from templates with your client's data, and webhooks that tell your client's system when an agreement is signed, so signed documents and field data return to it.
SG09.evidence: When a subscribed event is triggered, Acrobat Sign constructs an HTTPS POST with a JSON body and delivers that to the URL specified.
SG09.tier: an enterprise or developer tier account

SG10.name: Acrobat Sign for Salesforce
SG10.src: Adobe Help: Acrobat Sign for Salesforce installation guide
SG10.scope: Install and configure the Acrobat Sign for Salesforce package in your client's Salesforce org: permission sets, agreement templates with data mappings and merge fields, and buttons that send for signature from a record.
SG10.evidence: You can get the app from the AppExchange, and it supports various Salesforce editions: Professional, Enterprise, Unlimited, Developer, and Performance.

SG11.name: Acrobat Sign for Microsoft 365 and Teams
SG11.src: Adobe Help: Adobe Acrobat Sign for Microsoft 365
SG11.scope: Deploy the Acrobat Sign add-ins for Teams, Outlook, Word and PowerPoint from the Microsoft admin center, connect them to your client's Acrobat Sign account, and show teams how to send and track agreements from the apps they work in.
SG11.evidence: Adobe Acrobat Sign for Microsoft 365 enables Microsoft Admins to deploy all three apps simultaneously through the Microsoft admin center or directly from the Microsoft AppSource.

SG12.name: Acrobat Sign for Workday
SG12.src: Adobe Help: Adobe Acrobat Sign for Workday installation guide
SG12.scope: Connect Acrobat Sign to your client's Workday tenant: the OAuth relationship, the business process steps that send documents for signature, and a service account for the Workday group.
SG12.evidence: Adobe Acrobat Sign for Workday: Installation Guide explains how to integrate Adobe Acrobat Sign into your Workday client.

MQ01.name: User groups, access and email opt-out
MQ01.src: Experience League: Get started with Adobe Marketo Qualifier
MQ01.scope: Create the Marketo Qualifier and Marketo Qualifier Admins user groups in your client's Admin Console with the names and product profile Adobe specifies, add the optional group for managers who read email performance reports, add the users, and set the opt-out footer that goes on every outbound email.
MQ01.evidence: Administrators who configure CRM connections, the Knowledge Center, and global email opt-out settings must also belong to the Marketo Qualifier Admins user group.

MQ02.name: CRM connection and field mapping
MQ02.scope: Work with your client's CRM administrator on the connected app or app registration and the read access it needs, enter the connection in Marketo Qualifier, and map the prospect, contact, account and opportunity fields representatives see, marking the ones they filter and target by.
MQ02.evidence: Inbound mapping controls which CRM fields Marketo Qualifier imports and where they appear.

MQ03.name: Outlook, calendars and booking links
MQ03.scope: Get each of your client's representatives connected: the Outlook mailbox and calendar, signature, meeting length, buffers, working hours and the booking link, plus an email drafting context that sets your client's tone and structure. Arrange the one-time Microsoft 365 administrator approval where your client requires it.
MQ03.evidence: The connection lets Marketo Qualifier send from your mailbox, recognize when a prospect replies, and schedule meetings on your calendar.

MQ04.name: Knowledge Center playbook
MQ04.src: Experience League: Marketo Qualifier, Admin settings
MQ04.scope: Gather your client's sales playbooks, ideal customer profiles, positioning guides and collateral, set the company name and URL, upload the documents and build the playbook, then test that drafted emails and chat answers use your client's messaging.
MQ04.evidence: Upload sales plays, ideal customer profiles (ICPs), positioning guides, and other sales collateral in PDF, PPTX, or DOCX format.

MQ05.name: First Outbound Workflows
MQ05.src: Experience League: Marketo Qualifier, Outbound Workflows
MQ05.scope: Build your client's first Outbound Workflows with its sales leaders: the goal, targeting filters, the cadence of email, phone and LinkedIn steps, touchpoint prompts, send window, time zone and sharing. Review the first generated emails and the AI's reasoning with representatives before anyone is enrolled.
MQ05.evidence: An Outbound Workflow is a goal-driven outreach cadence. You define the goal and targeting criteria. AI then proposes a multitouch cadence and writes personalized email content for each prospect.

MQ07.name: Training for representatives, managers and administrators
MQ07.scope: Train your client's representatives on the prospect and account views, reviewing and approving drafts, the task queue for calls, LinkedIn InMails and email reviews, AI Chat and reply suggestions; train managers on outbound performance, and administrators on the settings.
MQ07.evidence: Use Tasks to complete the actions generated by Outbound Workflows. Select a task, take action, mark the task complete, and continue to the next task without leaving the page.

MQ08.name: Monthly outreach review and playbook upkeep
MQ08.src: Experience League: Outbound performance in Adobe Marketo Qualifier
MQ08.scope: Each month, review open, click, reply and meeting results by workflow and by representative with your client's sales leaders, tune goals and touchpoint prompts, duplicate and revise workflows that underperform, and refresh the Knowledge Center playbook.
MQ08.evidence: To track outbound activity and results across your team, select Outbound performance in the left navigation.

MQ06.name: Prospect list imports
MQ06.scope: Prepare and import prospect lists that are not in your client's CRM from CSV files, with the CRM lead ID where there is one and custom columns mapped so generated emails can use them.
MQ06.evidence: Map any custom or additional CSV fields, not only the standard ones.

MO01.name: Access, roles and sandbox permissions
MO01.src: Experience League: User access and permissions (Marketo Optimizer)
MO01.scope: Set up access for your client's team: the product profile and user groups in the Admin Console, the administrator, all-access and read-only roles in Experience Platform Permissions with the Marketo Optimizer sandbox on each, and the product permissions each role needs.
MO01.evidence: For each user type, you create a user group in the Admin Console and a role in Experience Platform, and then add the group to the role.

MO02.name: Email sending setup and channel configurations
MO02.scope: Delegate your client's sending subdomain to Adobe with the fully delegated or CNAME method, set the DMARC policy and check SPF and DKIM, review the IP pool, create an email channel configuration for each brand, region and message type, and have IT allowlist the sending addresses.
MO02.evidence: Create one or more email channel configurations that bind a subdomain, IP pool, and sender identity.

MO03.name: Program types, folders and tokens
MO03.scope: Define the program types your client's marketing needs, with their attributes, status steps and success statuses, set up the folder and program structure, and create the My Tokens that folders and programs inherit.
MO03.evidence: Program types define important aspects of programs and their members, and distinguish different types of marketing programs from each other.

MO04.name: People lists, personas and engagement scoring
MO04.scope: Build your client's dynamic and static people lists with filters on activity, company and person attributes, use the derived persona and the person engagement score as filters, and set the engagement score weighting model that fits how your client's leads behave.
MO04.evidence: In Adobe Marketo Optimizer, people lists are the person-level audience containers for targeting and person journey entry, with dynamic lists for rule-based live qualification and static lists for fixed or journey-managed membership.

MO05.name: First person journeys
MO05.scope: Design and publish your client's first person journeys inside their programs: the audience entry by dynamic list or by event, the wait, split and listen-for-event steps, the email actions and data changes, the start and end dates and the re-entry settings, then check each journey before it goes live.
MO05.evidence: In Adobe Marketo Optimizer, person journeys are automated, multistep lead-based marketing plans that orchestrate personalized experiences across channels.

MO06.name: Email templates, fragments and content rules
MO06.src: Experience League: Template content governance (Marketo Optimizer)
MO06.scope: Build your client's email templates and reusable visual fragments in the design space, lock the headers, logos and legal content that authors must not change, set up personalization with fallback text, and write the first published emails.
MO06.evidence: Content locking allows template authors to define governance rules that restrict which parts of an email template can be modified when the template is used in an email.

MO12.name: Team training and handover
MO12.scope: Train your client's marketers on the home page, the marketing workspace, programs, people lists, journeys and email authoring, with a short guide to your client's naming rules and a checklist for publishing.
MO12.evidence: Use the Home page in Adobe Marketo Optimizer to start AI conversations, launch skills, and open marketing workspaces.

MO07.name: AI path decisions and journey traffic control
MO07.src: Experience League: Journey traffic control (Marketo Optimizer)
MO07.scope: Add next best path steps to your client's journeys with a prompt for each path, run simulations on a sample audience and tune the prompts, then turn on journey traffic control for overlapping journeys: the importance of each scoring dimension, the journey descriptions the model reads, and a simulation before the weights go live.
MO07.evidence: Journey traffic control (JTC) prioritizes the best journey for a person when audiences overlap.

MO08.name: Landing pages and forms
MO08.scope: Set up the landing page subdomain and presets, create the form presets with their streaming connection and dataset in Experience Platform, then build and publish your client's standard forms and the landing pages that carry them.
MO08.evidence: Before marketers can create and publish forms to use in their landing pages, a product administrator must create one or more dedicated presets.

MO09.name: WhatsApp channel
MO09.src: Experience League: WhatsApp channel configuration (Marketo Optimizer)
MO09.scope: Connect your client's WhatsApp Business Account: the API credentials, the webhooks with opt-in, opt-out and help keywords and replies, and the channel configuration, then build the first WhatsApp messages from templates Meta has approved and add them to journeys.
MO09.evidence: Before marketers can create WhatsApp messages for person journeys, a product administrator must configure a WhatsApp channel.
MO09.ext: A WhatsApp Business Account with Meta

MO10.name: Message frequency and quiet hours rules
MO10.scope: Agree with your client how often a person may be contacted and at what hours, build the channel rule sets with frequency caps and quiet hours, activate them and apply them to the email actions in journeys.
MO10.evidence: Set frequency caps by channel and communication type to limit how many messages a profile receives and avoid overwhelming customers with similar communications.

MO11.name: Send-time optimization and conditional content
MO11.scope: Turn on send-time optimization for the email actions where timing matters, with the delivery window and the wait step Adobe requires, and build conditional content rules so one email shows a different block to each persona or segment.
MO11.evidence: Use the Send-time optimization (STO) feature to personalize email delivery timing for person journeys by predicting when each profile is most likely to engage.

MO13.name: Monthly journey and audience reviews
MO13.src: Experience League: Generate analytics reports (Marketo Optimizer)
MO13.scope: Each month, review your client's journey results, email performance, list membership and traffic control decisions, tune audiences, path prompts and score weights, and report findings and next steps.
MO13.evidence: Use it in the Coworker chat interface to explore activity trends, email performance, lead and account data, segment and list membership, and journey metrics.

XA28.name: Implementation plan from Coworker, checked against the tenant
XA28.src: Experience League: Plan Your Customer Journey Analytics or Streaming Media Implementation with Coworker
XA28.scope: Run Coworker's implementation guide skill with your client's team for one path (Customer Journey Analytics from scratch, the Adobe Analytics upgrade, Content Analytics, Marketing Campaign Analytics or Streaming Media), check each planned step against the live tenant (licenses, sandboxes, schemas, datasets, report suites and permissions), correct the owners and effort, and import the plan into Workfront or Jira as the delivery plan.
XA28.evidence: These skills don’t access your Adobe systems or make any changes. They help you plan your implementation. They don’t perform it or verify it against a live tenant.

XA29.name: Adobe Analytics and CJA data validation and fixes
XA29.src: Experience League: Validate Adobe Analytics to Customer Journey Analytics Data
XA29.scope: After your client completes the upgrade steps, run Coworker's validation skill on up to three report suite and data view pairs (a full audit compares up to 40 metrics and 20 dimensions), check each suggested action, and fix the causes in Experience Platform, Adobe Analytics or the data view, such as bot filtering, session settings, marketing channel derived fields, duplicate datasets or field mappings. Rerun until each pair reaches the agreed matching rate, and document the differences that are expected by design, such as device-based visitors against people.
XA29.evidence: Verify that the suggested actions are valid, then resolve them in Adobe Experience Platform or Adobe Analytics.

XA30.name: Coworker analytics enablement on CJA data views
XA30.src: Experience League: Analyze Analytics Data with Adobe CX Enterprise Coworker Chat

XA30.evidence: Create a library of vetted prompts and skills that correlate with the data and components that are available to users.

XA31.name: Streaming Media collection from the Coworker plan
XA31.src: Experience League: Plan Your Customer Journey Analytics or Streaming Media Implementation with Coworker
XA31.scope: Instrument your client's video or audio players for Streaming Media collection on the Edge, from the plan Coworker's implementation guide skill produces: configure the datastream and the XDM schema and dataset for media events, implement the SDK or API on up to two player platforms, map the media event model, add the media components to the CJA data view where CJA reports, and check that sessions, pings and completions reach CJA or Adobe Analytics reporting.
XA31.evidence: Get an implementation plan for Streaming Media collection on the Edge, covering datastream configuration, per-platform SDK/API implementation, and the media event model, so you correctly instrument sessions, pings, and completions for Customer Journey Analytics and/or Adobe Analytics reporting.

RC01.name: Real-Time CDP audience analysis in CJA
RC01.scope: Configure audience analysis by choosing the sandbox, merge policy, connection and data views (Adobe then creates the lookup dataset, audience dimensions and data view settings), and extend Adobe's Audience overview template with your client's KPIs.
RC01.evidence: Audience analysis allows you to ingest audience membership data from Experience Platform Profile datasets into a Customer Journey Analytics connection.

references.title: Analyze Experience Platform Audiences In Customer Journey Analytics

RC02.name: Identity and audience count alignment
RC02.src: Consistency of metrics and audience membership
RC02.scope: Align the CJA person ID and stitching method with the Real-Time CDP identity graph, agree which datasets and retention windows each app uses, and document expected audience count differences for stakeholders.
RC02.evidence: Real-time CDP and Customer Journey Analytics do not share the same definition of a person today.

RC03.name: Journey audiences from CJA for activation
RC03.src: Experience League: Create and publish audiences
RC03.scope: Define up to five audiences from cross-channel journey behavior in CJA, publish them to Experience Platform, and set up their activation in Real-Time CDP with your client.
RC03.evidence: Audiences you define in Customer Journey Analytics can be published to Adobe Experience Platform

JC01.name: Journey data in the main CJA connection
JC01.scope: Add the Journey Optimizer datasets to your client's main CJA connection with web, app and offline data in a separate data view, leaving Adobe's auto-created connection and data view untouched so Journey Optimizer's own reports keep working.
JC01.evidence: Or you can add Journey Optimizer datasets to an existing connection.
JC01.tier: CJA Select or higher (more than one event dataset in a connection)

JC02.name: Journey and experiment analysis in CJA
JC02.src: Adobe Customer Journey Analytics & Adobe Journey Optimizer integration
JC02.scope: Build Workspace projects that tie journeys and messages to web, app and offline conversions, configure the experiment and variant dimensions with their Experimentation context labels, and build Experimentation panel reports for journey content experiments.
JC02.evidence: Customer Journey Analytics data views and analysis provide campaign and journey insight.

TC01.name: Target reporting setup in CJA
TC01.src: Target reporting in Adobe Customer Journey Analytics
TC01.scope: Add the event dataset and the Adobe Target Classification Events lookup dataset (created by Adobe) to a CJA connection, then add activity and experience dimensions with persistence and the Experimentation context labels. Before each launch, confirm the activity type is supported and its reporting source is CJA with the agreed data view, since it can't change once live.
TC01.evidence: configure persistence for the Activity Name and Activity ID dimensions

TC02.name: Experiment reports in Workspace
TC02.src: Target reporting in Adobe Customer Journey Analytics
TC02.scope: Build Experimentation panel reports and a reusable Workspace template for Target activities, showing lift and confidence on your client's CJA success metrics.
TC02.evidence: Activity reports must be built in Customer Journey Analytics.

TC04.name: CJA audiences for Target, through Real-Time CDP or Journey Optimizer
TC04.scope: Publish people audiences from CJA to Experience Platform and share them through the Adobe Target destination under a Real-Time CDP or Journey Optimizer entitlement. For same-page or next-page use, validate a datastream with both Adobe Target and Adobe Experience Platform enabled and an active-on-edge merge policy for edge audiences. Without a datastream, verify next-session use only.
TC04.evidence: The Adobe Target destination is now available to organizations with Adobe Journey Optimizer, in addition to organizations with Real-Time CDP.

TC03.name: A4T to CJA reporting transition
TC03.src: Experience League: Target reporting in Adobe Customer Journey Analytics
TC03.scope: Where your client is on Analytics for Target today, choose which activity types move to CJA reporting, set the reporting source per activity or account wide, and give Target users the Experience Platform role they need.
TC03.evidence: This functionality is comparable to what is performed in Adobe Analytics (AA) via Analytics for Target (A4T)

OX1.src: Experience League: Brand Visibility, CDN log forwarding

OX2.src: Experience League: Brand Visibility, other log providers
